description: Introducing Rolled Clay! A brand-new alphabet with a soft, hand-rolled look — like someone shaped each letter from a coil of clay. Natural, organic, with a smooth finish. It's perfect for nurseries, kids' rooms, name signs, and anywhere you want a warm, handmade touch. Each letter prints flat with no supports and looks beautiful in any color. These look great straight off the print bed with a matte finish, or with some basic sanding and painting you can mimic the popular ceramic glaze finish. These print easily with blu tack or mounting tape, and are lightweight and far less fragile than traditional ceramics. Commercial License Info - Want to Sell Prints? These designs are free to download and print for personal use. If you'd like to sell prints commercially — on Etsy, at markets, or in your own shop — a commercial license is available through my Patreon Meet the Sister Set: Flat Clay Rolled Clay has a chunkier cousin! Flat Clay takes this same organic style and presses it soft and smooth — a fuller, but flatter look from the same family. Flat Clay is available exclusively to my Patreon Pro members (not on MakerWorld). Print Instructions Open the file in Bambu Studio. Delete the letters you do not need. Select all of the remaining letters and resize them as needed. (If you resize, make sure to reset the adaptive layers!) Use the “Arrange All Objects” function to rearrange the remaining letters for printing. Slice and Print! Paint Instructions While these look great off the print bed, (especially in a matte PLA), they also look phenomenal when painted. Others have also had great success with UV Resin applied directly to colored prints. I've included instructions below for how we paint our models. I've included a photo of the end results on some of my other models. After printing, sand with sandpaper progressing from low grit to high grit. (I used 100-180-220) Clean thoroughly. Paint with Primer ( I used Rustoleum 2-in-1 Automotive Primer) After primer is dry, sand again with 400 grit sandpaper. Clean thoroughly again. Paint with 3-4 coats of your preferred paint, (I used Rustoleum 2X in a Satin). Finish with 3-4 coats of clear coat, (I used Rustoleum 2X in Gloss).

Print each plate one by one Use a clean print plate with some glue (unless you are using a super tack plate) Use dried out filament (Different filament types impact the print differently, please adjust your settings accordingly) The Sculpture Lid needs support and will have a “fake bottom” under the lid that needs to be removed. It might come of by itself when removing from the print plate, if it doesn't, use pliers - just "digg in"/grab and start to pull - it should come of pretty easy. Remove the support using pliers. Gently breake them off starting at the top around the flag - hold the flag securing between two fingers with one hand when you remove the support around the flag. Move to the dragon and unicorn - start at the top around the horns and wings, the rest should come of easy. Printing Instructions Important: Please leave each object on its dedicated build plate. Different filament types impact the print differently, please adjust your settings accordingly. Support Removal Let the model cool down before removing the supports. Use pliers when removing the supports. Start with breaking the support in the middle by “crushing” them by using a plier. This helps loosen the structure before removing the supports. Gently wiggle the support until it starts to loosen, then pull downward. Start carefully at the top around the hand and flags . Hold the hand and flags securely between two fingers with one hand while gently breaking away the support with the other hand. Take your time around the small details to avoid damaging the fine features. Begin around the delicate features first, especially the horns and wings. The remaining support should come off more easily. It also prints with a temporary “fake bottom” underneath the lid, which must be removed after printing. The Sculpture lid will look strange when you start to print it as it layers “loose curls" as support for the bottom that almost looks like it's failing but it's all as it should be. description: The Overachiever: Fur & Chill 4" Edition I designed the Fur & Chill 6" Edition first. Then I tested a 4" fan out of curiosity. I didn't expect much. 130 CFM vs 345 CFM is not a fair fight on paper. Turns out fluid dynamics had other plans. The 4" fan's higher velocity through a smaller duct punches through the HEPA filter more efficiently than the higher volume 6" fan. Pair that with a redesigned oval nozzle and the result is strong, directed airflow in a quieter, more compact, and cheaper package. This is my recommended version for most people. That said, the 6" isn't obsolete. If you run it on a larger bed, want maximum volume of air moving under the covers, or just sleep like you're trying to recreate a wind tunnel, the 6" still delivers. But for a typical setup where you want effective cooling without waking your partner with fan noise, the 4" is the sweet spot. The Problem BUT WAIT — THERE'S MORE AIRFLOW! (Somehow) Got hot flashes? Partner stealing all the cool air? Just generally melting into your mattress like a forgotten popsicle? I have a solution for you. It only requires a printer, some filament, and the willingness to spend way too many evenings measuring air velocity with an anemometer like a completely normal person. I stumbled across Paul 2 Travel's brilliant Bed Rocket and immediately thought, "yes, this is exactly what I need." Except I share a house with an 86lb drooling fur monster whose entire life purpose appears to be shedding, and a cat who bullies both of us. Pointing a fan at your bed while living with these two is less "refreshing sleep experience" and more "marinating in a fur tornado all night." Fur & Chill was inspired by Paul 2 Travel's Bed Rocket, which is still a fantastic solution if you don't need filtration and want something that uses less filament. Go give it a look. What Fan Do I Need? Vivosun 4" inline fan : Affordable, widely available, and apparently better at this than it has any right to be. Tested filter: Levoit Core 300 replacement filter, widely available, affordable, with multiple compatible third-party options if you want to save a few dollars. A Note on Filters Not all HEPA filters are created equal for this application. I tested a Shop-Vac HEPA filter and it decimated airflow. Shop-Vac filters are optimized for suction, not continuous airflow from an inline fan. Expect 85%+ airflow loss. Hard pass. Stick to a dedicated air purifier HEPA filter . These are designed for consistent airflow resistance and work significantly better with inline fans. I also tested the Levoit Core Mini filter hoping for a more compact option. It reduced airflow to a very gentle breeze. If there's demand I'm happy to upload an adapter for it, but expect lighter airflow. Assembly Instructions Step 1 — Filter & Canister Drop the HEPA filter into the canister. Attach the adapter to the top of the canister (it's a tight fit, expect to “pop” it in) Step 2 — Fan Slide the collar/skirt onto the fan, then press the fan into the adapter until seated. There are markings on the fan to tell you which direction air flows. Step 3 — Ductwork Connect the long cylinder to the top of the fan. If additional height is needed, attach the optional height extender first (not pictured). Connect the first 45° elbow to the cylinder, then attach the second 45° elbow to the first. Step 4 — Nozzle & Base Attach the nozzle to the final elbow. Set the completed assembly into the leg ring base and orient the nozzle toward the head of the bed.

Mit diesem Modell kann man die Midea Portasplit reversibel auf einen 2-Wege Kondenswasser Betrieb umbauen, ohne das Gerät selbst zu verändern und Garantieverlust zu riskieren. Den Schlauch vom Wassertank an den unteren Anschluss anstecken. Nun die Abdeckung unten auf die 2 Riegel stecken und mit den Originalschrauben oben festschrauben. Nun kann man wählen ob das Wasser wie üblich ans Außengerät gepumpt werden soll (Stellung “out”), oder durch den neuen Schlauch in einen Kanister oder Waschbecken, etc. (Stellung “in”. Diese Umbau bietet sich an, wenn sich z.B. wie bei mir eine Terrasse mit Loungeecke direkt unter dem Außengerät befindet, so dass das Kondenswasser nicht einfach außen abgelassen werden kann. Trotec PAC 2010 E Abluftadapter fürs Fenster – 142 mm / 150 mm Bajonett-System Dies ist ein Abluftadapter-System für die mobile Klimaanlage Trotec PAC 2010 E . Ich habe das Modell entwickelt, um die übliche Stoff-Fensterabdichtung durch eine stabilere und sauberere Lösung zu ersetzen. Als Fenstereinsatz verwende ich eine 6 mm Stegplatte / Hohlkammerplatte aus Polycarbonat . Das System besteht aus einer festen Basis an der Fensterplatte und wechselbaren Bajonett-Aufsätzen. Dadurch kann der Fenstereinsatz montiert bleiben, während man den Schlauchadapter oder den Verschlussdeckel später einfach wechseln kann. Kurze Bauteilübersicht Teil A – Innenflansch mit universellem Bajonettverschluss Teil A ist die feste Basis auf der Innenseite der Stegplatte. Es bleibt dauerhaft am Fenstereinsatz montiert und enthält die universelle Bajonettaufnahme. Die Teile B142, B150 und D passen alle in diesen Bajonettverschluss. Zusätzlich ist ein offenes Gitter integriert, damit Katzen nicht durch die Öffnung entkommen können, wenn kein Schlauch montiert ist. Teil B142 – Adapter für den originalen Trotec-Schlauch Teil B142 ist der Adapter für den originalen Abluftschlauch des Trotec PAC 2010 E. Der Schlauch hat bei mir ca. 142 mm Außendurchmesser über den Rillen . Diese Version habe ich selbst gedruckt und getestet. Der Schlauch wird in das gedruckte Innengewinde eingedreht. Teil B150 – Optionaler Adapter für 150-mm-Schlauch Teil B150 ist eine alternative Version für einen 150-mm-Abluftschlauch. Der Bajonettanschluss ist identisch zu B142 und passt daher ebenfalls in Teil A. Diese Version ist im Modell enthalten, wurde von mir aber noch nicht selbst gedruckt oder getestet . Bitte vor dem Druck unbedingt den echten Schlauchdurchmesser messen, da viele 150-mm-Schläuche die 150 mm als Nennmaß oder Innendurchmesser angeben. Teil C – Außen-Gegenring Teil C sitzt auf der Außenseite der Stegplatte. Teil A und Teil C werden durch die 6-mm-Steegplatte miteinander verschraubt und klemmen die Platte zwischen sich ein. Teil C hat ebenfalls ein offenes Gitter und Taschen für M3-Muttern. Teil D – Verschlussdeckel / Winterdeckel Teil D ist der abnehmbare Deckel für den Bajonettverschluss, wenn kein Abluftschlauch angeschlossen ist. Er nutzt denselben Bajonettanschluss wie die Schlauchadapter. Die Mitte ist geschlossen und der Deckel hat einen größeren Griff, damit man ihn besser drehen und entfernen kann. Getestete Version Ich habe persönlich die Version B142 für den originalen Trotec-Schlauch gedruckt und getestet. Gemessene Schlauchmaße des originalen Trotec-Schlauchs: Außendurchmesser über den Rillen: ca. 142 mm Innendurchmesser: ca. 128 mm Rillenabstand / Pitch: ca. 10 mm Die B150-Version ist zusätzlich enthalten, wurde von mir aber noch nicht getestet. Warum ein Gitter integriert ist In Teil A und Teil C ist ein offenes Gitter integriert. Das Gitter dient vor allem als einfache Sicherheit, falls der Schlauch nicht montiert ist. So können Katzen nicht einfach durch die Öffnung nach draußen gelangen. Das Gitter ist bewusst relativ offen gehalten, damit der Luftstrom der Klimaanlage möglichst wenig behindert wird. Verwendetes Material Ich habe die Teile mit folgendem Material gedruckt: Bambu Lab PETG HF Farbe: Weiß Ich empfehle PETG oder ein anderes temperaturbeständigeres Material. PLA würde ich nicht empfehlen, da der Abluftschlauch und der Bereich am Fenster warm werden können. Verwendete Schrauben und Muttern Zur Befestigung von Teil A und Teil C an der Stegplatte habe ich verwendet: M3-Schrauben M3-Muttern Die gedruckten Teile haben Taschen für M3-Muttern. Ich habe die Muttern mit 3D-Drucker-Kleber in die Taschen eingeklebt. Das hat bei mir sehr gut funktioniert. Fenstereinsatz / Stegplatte Als Fenstereinsatz habe ich eine Stegplatte von Bauhaus verwendet: Bauhaus Hohlkammerplatte ECO UV https://www.bauhaus.info/hohlkammerplatten/hohlkammerplatte-eco-uv/p/28541981 Die gekaufte Platte hatte folgende Maße: 2000 × 980 mm 6 mm Dicke Ich habe die Platte passend für mein Fenster zugeschnitten. Danach habe ich das große runde Loch für den Adapter ausgeschnitten und die Schraublöcher manuell mit einem Schraubenzieher gemacht. Meine fertige Fensterplatte hatte ungefähr folgende Maße: 1460 mm Höhe 860 mm Breite 6 mm Dicke Montagehinweise Stegplatte passend für das Fenster zuschneiden. Großes rundes Loch für den Abluftadapter ausschneiden. M3-Schraublöcher herstellen. M3-Muttern in die dafür vorgesehenen Muttertaschen der gedruckten Teile einsetzen. Die M3-Muttern bei Bedarf mit etwas 3D-Drucker-Kleber, Sekundenkleber oder einem geeigneten Kunststoffkleber in den Taschen fixieren. Ich habe die Muttern eingeklebt, damit sie bei der Montage nicht herausfallen. Das hat bei mir sehr gut funktioniert. Teil A auf der Innenseite der Platte einsetzen. Teil C auf der Außenseite der Platte einsetzen. Teil A und Teil C mit M3-Schrauben und M3-Muttern durch die Platte verschrauben. Without a limit stopper on the end of the blind cord, the cord will swing wildly when windows are opened for ventilation. It easily tangles with curtain tracks and window frames, and even poses entanglement risks for kids. This model targets this pain point, firmly locking the cord end and fundamentally restricting large-range swinging of the pull cord. Upgrade Highlight: Threaded Lock Mounting Mechanism The original version adopted an integrated snap-fit structure, which was hard to install & remove and prone to loosening after long-term pulling. This new upgraded split threaded locking system consists of a textured anti-slip knob and pulley bracket. For installation: Thread the cord through the pulley then tighten the knob. The threaded structure delivers even, stable clamping force. To detach, simply twist the knob counterclockwise without forcing or damaging the part—easy enough for elderly users to operate independently. Granular anti-slip texture is added to the thread contact surface to prevent slipping even with damp hands, and the threads resist stripping after repeated long-term use. Structural & 3D Printing Advantages 1. Integrated Smooth Pulley Groove: Rounded inner slot protects the pull cord from sharp edges, reducing abrasion and extending the service life of nylon blind cords. 3. Support-Free Printing Geometry: No complex overhangs across the whole model. It can be printed directly on consumer FDM 3D printers without extra support structures, lowering print failure rates. Standard PLA filament provides sufficient strength for indoor long-term use, with good heat and aging resistance. Compatibility Fits most standard woven nylon pull cords for household roller blinds. Tolerance is reserved in the design, so cords with minor thickness differences can be securely clamped. Application Scenarios Suitable for all manual roller blinds, zebra blinds and shangri-la blinds in bedrooms, living rooms and studies. Create high-quality custom trays for gifts, organization, or home decor. This project was developed to offer maximum flexibility: simply adjust the dimensions, and the script seamlessly recalculates the heart border distribution, maintaining a flawless geometry designed for support-free 3D printing. Perfect for both personal use and the production of unique, exclusive pieces. --- CUSTOMIZATION --- The model is designed so that any user can configure it quickly, with the number of hearts being automatically calculated to fill the entire perimeter! 1. Basic Settings - Tray Length & Width: Maximum exterior dimensions of the tray (mm). - Base Thickness: Thickness of the base along the Z-axis. - Cut Inner Hearts: Enables boolean subtraction to remove the inner portion of the hearts, yielding a smooth interior wall. - Alternating Layers: Enables horizontal offset (half-step) on even layers, aligning geometry in a brick pattern. - Number of Layers: Quantity of heart rings stacked along the Z-axis. - Heart Base Size: Size of the heart (mm). The script recalculates the perimeter and automatically adjusts the instance count. 2. Engraving & Text Settings - Enable Top Text: Adds embossed (raised) text to the center of the base's top face. - Enable Bottom Logo: Adds debossed (engraved) text to the base's bottom face. 3. Advanced Settings For users who want fine-grained control over mesh and placement: - Heart Width / Thickness / Height Ratio: Individual scale of the heart on its local X, Y, and Z axes. - Heart Size Multiplier: Global scale (XYZ) applied to the heart. - Heart Facing Rotation: Angular rotation (local Z-axis) of each heart at its origin. - Heart Z Offset: Z-axis displacement of the heart layers. Negative values intersect with Z=0 (cut plane), generating a flat bed adhesion area. - Heart Radial Offset: Radial displacement of the anchor line. Negative values increase volumetric intersection with the base. - Lateral and Vertical Overlap Factor: Interpenetration rate between adjacent instances. --- TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS & PRINTING --- - Clean Printing Base: The parametric bottom is cut perfectly flat on the Z-axis, ensuring maximum bed adhesion without the fragility of the heart tips. - Support-Free: The design ensures progressive overhangs without the need for any supports in FDM printing. - Premium Finish Tip: For a wonderful textured ceramic look, enable the "Fuzzy Skin" option on the outer contour in your slicer! RECOMMENDED PRINT SETTINGS (Bambu Studio / OrcaSlicer) --- - Layer Height: 0.16mm (Optimal for the vertical curves of the spheres) - Wall Generator: Arachne (Recommended for filling small fusions) - Infill: 10% Gyroid or Cross Hatch - Supports: No supports needed! - Fuzzy Skin (Optional for premium finish): Contour, Thickness: 0.3mm, Point distance: 0.8mm 💡 Pro Tip: Enable Variable/Adaptive Layer Height in your slicer.

Summary This project is designed to germinate Chia seeds, although other small seeds can also be used. A spray can be used to moisten the sprouts a couple of times a day, but in my case it was not necessary. Although Chia sprouts can be consumed as food, we recommend that in this case the impression be made with filaments approved for this purpose. description: Hold a medically accurate piece of human anatomy right in your hands! (Read the last sentence for a curiosity question!) 🩻 Overview 🩻 This advanced 3D model is a highly detailed representation of the human shoulder (glenohumeral) joint, developed through a hybrid medical and digital workflow. The skeletal framework was extracted directly from real CT scans to ensure an anatomically correct bone morphology. The surrounding soft tissues were subsequently hand-modeled in Blender, carefully crafted based on anatomical studies and medical literature. To ensure the best possible 3D printing experience and educational clarity, this model focuses on the primary structures. Some minor or overlapping anatomical elements were intentionally omitted, providing a clean, understandable, and highly printable display piece without overwhelming the slicer or the viewer. 🦴 Included Anatomical Structures The model highlights the key bony landmarks and major soft tissues crucial for understanding shoulder biomechanics: Skeletal Framework (CT Extracted): Scapula (Shoulder Blade), Clavicle (Collarbone), and Humerus (Upper arm bone), featuring accurate articular surfaces and bone topography. 💪 Muscular System (Blender Modeled): Key musculature, including major components of the rotator cuff and biceps, which are essential for shoulder stability and movement. 🔗 Ligaments & Connective Tissue (Blender Modeled): Essential stabilizing ligaments and capsular elements highlighting the articulation points. 🎯 Intended Use Education & Study: A brilliant hands-on visual aid for medical students, anatomy classes, and healthcare professionals. Clinical Communication: Perfect for physical therapists and orthopedic specialists to easily explain shoulder mechanics, impingements, or rotator cuff injuries to their patients. Advanced 3D Printing Showcase: A fantastic display piece that highlights the precision of your printer on complex organic shapes. 💡 Print Settings & Recommendations Material: This model has been fully designed and optimized for standard PLA . No flexible or exotic filaments are required. Versatile Print Profiles: To make this model accessible to everyone, I will be uploading dedicated print profiles for both AMS and non-AMS setups . The multicolor profile is organized to maximize visual contrast and educational value. Based on the provided images, the recommended color mapping is: Bone White: Skeletal structures (Scapula, Clavicle, Humerus) and tendons. Red: Musculature (Rotator cuff and supporting muscles). Blue: Ligaments, and capsular structures. Different colors are presented in the non-AMS setup for printing reasons. SIMPLY INSTRUCTIONS FOR THE NO-AMS PROFILE ⚠️ Disclaimer: This model is intended strictly for educational, illustrative, and hobbyist purposes. It is not a clinical tool and does not replace professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. For the most interested ones, a bit of anatomy! 🤓🫀🔬 The shoulder, or shoulder girdle, is a complex system designed to give the upper limb a very wide range of motion, with bones, muscles, tendons, and ligaments working together. In my model, the labeled parts show both the supporting framework and the soft tissues that stabilize movement. Bones 🦴 The scapula is a flat triangular bone at the back of the thorax, and it provides attachment for many shoulder muscles. The humerus is the upper arm bone, and its rounded head articulates with the scapula to form the glenohumeral joint, which is the main shoulder joint. The clavicle acts like a strut between the sternum and the scapula, helping keep the shoulder positioned away from the chest wall so the arm can move freely. Soft tissues 💪 The rotator cuff is made of four muscles and their tendons, and its main job is to keep the head of the humerus centered while the arm moves and rotates. The tendons connect muscle to bone, and the long head of the biceps tendon also contributes to shoulder stability as it passes near the joint. The ligaments connect bone to bone and reinforce the joint capsule, helping prevent excessive movement and instability. The subacromial bursa is a small fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between the acromion and the rotator cuff tendons during arm elevation. A question for the more curious viewer: Why does the biceps tendon anchor to the scapula instead of attaching directly to the humerus? Let me know in the comments!

model_name: alphabet handwriting stencil with stroke direction
description: Support young learners in mastering correct letter formation with this all-in-one stencil plate featuring the complete lowercase alphabet! Based on the NSW Foundation font and designed for early writers, each letter features directional arrows and stroke numbers cut into the surface to guide proper handwriting formation - all 26 letters on a single, easy-to-use board. Thoughtfully Designed for Young Learners In stencil letters like a, b, d, e, g, o, p, q and others, small bridge points are needed to keep the inner parts of the letter connected to the plate. In many stencils these bridges are placed arbitrarily, interrupting the natural flow of the letter mid-stroke. In this design, the bridges are deliberately positioned at each letter's starting or ending point — so when a child begins tracing, they start at the bridge and follow the letter all the way around. The result is an uninterrupted tracing experience that teaches correct stroke formation, not just the shape of the letter. Print Options The arrows and stroke numbers are cut out of each letter — in a single colour they're still clearly visible and functional. For the best visual result, the colour change is already set in the slicer file at the correct layer height, so no manual configuration is needed. If you have an AMS , it will handle the filament swap automatically. No AMS? No problem — your printer will pause and prompt you to swap filament manually at the right moment. The result is a contrasting colour on the arrows and stroke numbers, making the letter outlines really pop. Print Tips Due to the fine details in this model, good bed adhesion is critical — poor adhesion can cause lifting or warping and ruin the small details. 🧼 Clean your plate thoroughly with hot water and dishwashing liquid before printing and allow to dry completely 🖼️ An outer brim is included in the slicer profile to prevent warping and lifting on this large, flat print. If you have adhesion issues on the insides of the letters, reslice with inner brims turned on. 🗼 Prime tower is disabled — this is intentional, so don't be alarmed when you don't see one in the preview Coming Soon A face-down version with coloured inserts is in development; the same great stencil with a premium finish. Follow my profile so you don't miss it! Also Check Out For individual letter pieces your child can pick up, arrange, and trace one at a time, head to my Stencil Puzzle Pieces — same font, same arrow system, same thoughtful bridge placement, but each letter is its own interlocking puzzle tile. Perfect for name recognition, word-building, and sorting games alongside this stencil. Browse my other models for more Foundation font tools designed for early learners.

Product Description The WindFlux is a purely mechanical wind measurement device that transforms wind speed into a dynamic visual signal—no electronics, no batteries, just precision engineering. At its core, a three-cup rotor captures wind energy and directly drives an integrated impulse drum. As the drum rotates behind a narrow viewing window, specially designed patterns generate a distinct optical pulse. Each wind speed range produces a unique visual rhythm—allowing intuitive interpretation at a glance. The system combines low-friction bearings, balanced rotor geometry, and a compact modular design for smooth operation even at low wind speeds. Its dual-subassembly construction ensures straightforward assembly and reliable alignment of all moving parts. 3D Printing Notes Recommended material: PETG, due to its superior weather resistance compared to PLA. No supports required – all parts are designed for clean, support-free printing. No screws or glue needed – the design relies entirely on press-fit connections. Printable without AMS (multi-material system): If printing in a single color, simply fill in the text fields and impulse bars afterward using a permanent marker for clear contrast. Reading and Interpreting Wind Speed WindFlux uses a three-zone impulse drum , where each zone is tuned to a specific wind speed range. As the drum rotates, you observe which zone produces a clear pulsation in the viewing window. 0–3 m/s (Low Wind Zone): The section with the finest pattern produces a distinct, slow pulsation . Individual transitions are visible and easy to follow. 3–7 m/s (Medium Wind Zone): The middle section generates a steady, rhythmic pulse , which is typically the most stable and clearly defined signal. >7 m/s (High Wind Zone): The section with the coarsest pattern produces a fast, compact pulsation , appearing more intense and slightly fused. How to Read It Instead of tracking position, you simply observe: Which zone shows the clearest, most stable pulsation If the fine pattern pulses clearly → low wind If the middle pattern dominates → moderate wind If the coarse pattern becomes most active → strong wind All three zones may be visible simultaneously, but only one will produce the most distinct pulse at a given wind speed. This makes interpretation fast, intuitive, and independent of numerical scales. Built for clarity, durability, and mechanical elegance, WindFlux offers a unique analog approach to wind indication—turning invisible airflow into a visible, tactile experience.

description: Help students pause, breathe, and reset with this tactile Wave Breathing Pause Card from 3DprintEDU. This 3D printable SEL tool gives children a calming finger tracing path to follow while practising mindful breathing, focus, and emotional regulation. Students begin at the raised O , then slowly trace along the wave paths as they breathe in and out. The included 3MF file contains both versions , so you can choose the style that works best for your students, classroom, or sensory space: Raised Path Version An embossed tactile wave path that students can feel clearly as they trace. Indented Path Version An engraved tactile wave path that gives students a smooth recessed channel to follow with their finger. Both versions are no AMS , quick to print, and use less than 20 g of filament, making them easy to print for classrooms, calm corners, counselling spaces, occupational therapy rooms, and home regulation kits. How to Use Begin at the raised O , which is designed to be the consistent starting point across the SEL Pause Cards collection. Place your finger on the O and slowly follow the wave path. Students can breathe in as they trace up each wave, then breathe out as they trace down each wave. The repeated wave pattern gives students a gentle rhythm to follow as they slow their breathing and refocus. Repeat the path a few times, moving calmly from wave to wave. description: Anatomy Pro: Interactive Bone Internal Structure Detailed Description Dive deep into human biology with this high-fidelity, multi-color educational model of a long bone (Femur/Humerus cross-section). This model is designed specifically for students, medical professionals, and science enthusiasts to visualize what lies beneath the "hard" surface of our skeletal system. The design features a strategic cutaway to reveal the complex layers of living tissue. It is an indispensable tool for classrooms or home-schooling environments where a 2D textbook image simply isn't enough to convey the 3D reality of biological architecture. Key Anatomical Features Included: Compact Bone: The dense, hard outer layer that provides strength. Spongy Bone (Cancellous): The intricate, porous lattice structure shown in the epiphysis. Bone Marrow: Represented by the central red core, the powerhouse of blood cell production. Epiphyseal Line: The visible "growth plate" remnant where the bone once lengthened. Blood Vessels: Detailed arterial and venous pathways (Red and Blue) showing how bone is a living, breathing organ. Print Settings & Material Recommendations To achieve the vibrant, anatomical accuracy seen in the photos, this model is optimized for multi-color printing (AMS/Unitree). Filament Recommendation: For the best results, I highly recommend using SUNLU Filament . Their tolerances are incredible for detailed anatomical prints like this. Bone Structure: SUNLU PLA Plus White – provides the perfect "bone" finish with superior strength. Marrow & Vessels: SUNLU PLA Meta Red and SUNLU PLA Meta Blue . The Meta series flows beautifully for those tiny vascular details. Pro Tip for Multi-Color: Since this is a color-intensive print, check out my tutorial: How to remesh and color prints effectively in Bambu Studio and/or Snapmaker U1 to minimize waste and maximize detail! History & Background This model was developed out of a need for affordable, tactile medical training aids. Traditional medical-grade bone models can cost hundreds of dollars. By 3D printing this design, educators can provide every student with a hands-on experience, allowing them to trace the path of blood vessels and feel the difference between the porous spongy bone and the solid compact bone. Remix Ideas & Expanded Use This model is a perfect base for several other projects: Pathology Remix: Modify the marrow or spongy bone area to show the effects of Osteoporosis or Leukemia for clinical demonstrations. TrailMark3D Turn Your Trail Into a Trophy TrailMark3D is a web application that generates 3D printable terrain models from GPX files. Upload any GPX track from Strava, Garmin, Komoot, or other tracking apps and get a detailed topographic model ready for 3D printing, zero setup, no software to install, no CAD skills required. Whether it's the summit you finally bagged, a century ride, a multi-day thru-hike, or your local loop, TrailMark3D turns the route you recorded into a physical object you can hold, display, or gift. Who It's For Hikers & trail runners who want a tangible keepsake of a route or summit Cyclists commemorating a big climb, gran fondo, or tour Gift-givers looking for something personal for the outdoor enthusiast in their life, or organizers and gift shops producing them in small batches for events and races. 3D printing hobbyists who want real-world terrain data without wrangling GIS tools How it Works Upload your GPX file to TrailMark3D.com Choose your preferred model shape, size , rotation, map features, printing style Generate your 3D terrain model (processing takes minutes depending on features, size, and resolution) Download the STL/3MF file for 3D printing Core Features Web application - No installation or boilerplate setup needed. Just upload, tweak, and generate. Shape options - Square, Circle, Hexagon Map features - Terrain, Buildings, Roads, Water Bodies, Trail (from GPX) Separated objects - Map features are separate objects inside the 3MF file, so objects can be printed separately. NO AMS NEEDED. Multi-day adventure workflow - Upload up to 5 GPX files to combine your multi-day hike, ride, or any recorded adventure. Job storage - Your latest generated 3D mesh is always stored in the database under your account, so you can always come back to redownload or modify your model. Persistent 3D mesh generation - 3D mesh generation can take time. This feature lets you close your browser and come back anytime to download the generated 3D model. Interactive 2D map view - Resize, rotate, or drag your choice of shape on a 2D map view. Selective water body removal - You may or may not want to print some of the fetched water bodies. This tool lets you exclude water body segments from being generated. Extension tiles - A single GPX is a single tile by default. You can extend the tiles by adding new tiles in the Interactive 2D Map View. Jigsaw puzzle - Generate up to a 20×20 jigsaw terrain puzzle with full control over the jigsaw shape parameters and randomness. Preset (Experimental) - Skip the tweaking by selecting the type of adventure for your GPX. Free & Pro Tiers The core features of TrailMark3D are completely free - no credit card, no expiry. With the free tier you get up to 10 downloads per month, grid resolution up to 200, all three shape options (Square, Circle, Hexagon), water features (Seas, Lakes, Rivers), through-hole water slots, water preview, tree line, activity presets, 3D trail animation, 3MF export, and custom colors. The free tier limits are set around what the server can sustainably handle - 10 downloads/month and a resolution cap of 200 keep things running smoothly for everyone without blowing past my hosting budget. Pro upgrades go directly toward the server capacity that makes higher limits possible. Upgrading to Pro unlocks everything in the free tier plus: unlimited downloads, grid resolution up to 500, shelf mode and water exclusion, shrink-below-trail, buildings and roads, multi-day trips (up to 5 days), priority processing, and early access to upcoming features. Why TrailMark3D From data to object - Your recorded route becomes a real, printable model with accurate terrain. Full control - Tune shape and which map features to include before you generate. Print-friendly - Separated objects mean clean multi-part prints without needing an AMS. Come back anytime - Generation runs server-side, and your jobs are saved to your account. Free to start - The core features are completely free, with Pro available when you need more power. Zero setup - No software to install, no CAD skills required. After many months of developing, it’s finally here! This is an Inline 2 Vacuum Engine, a model of an inline 2 internal combustion engine, that runs off a vacuum. I have spent months working out every little detail and mainly trying to get every tolerance perfect. I also go through a lot of work on all of my models to ensure that they are easy to print, and with minimal supports. This model is completely press-fit, no glue, no tape, no magnets, just plain old PLA, modeled with the intent of being easy and fun to assemble and mess with, for experts to beginners to people who just enjoy messing around with cool contraptions. Additionally, those who have previous experience with vacuum engines can attempt to performance tune it, by changing the offset the camshaft has on the crankshaft. Simply print out all the parts (don't forget to boost with that free boost token ;), assemble with the easy assembly instructions, and enjoy! Note: You will need six 608 bearings, either 3D printed versions from Makerworld, or the metal versions which I have included in the Bill of Materials from Makersupply. Also note that the tolerances are very good for a Bambu Lab A1, but I cannot guarantee perfect fits with other printers, although they should be pretty close. Operation Instructions: Operation is easy, simply stick a vacuum up to the cone on the exhaust manifold, and watch it rip! You may need to give it a rotate or two to help it get started. Tips for success: Be sure that the camshaft if offset by a quarter turn from the crankshaft (explained in the instructions). Try lubing all of the areas where there is filament on filament contact, to reduce friction and increase speed and power. Clean out your vacuum's filter, or remove it entirely to improve your vacuum performance. Be sure there is little friction inside the crank case, as in make sure there are tiny gaps between all of the moving parts to ensure they move freely. Updates: I have many updates planned, from gaskets cutouts, to new exhaust manifolds for different vacuums. I will include links to them here as they are developed. I just finished a throttle body for this engine, and you can find it here Thank you for checking this model out, and if you enjoyed, please share with your friends and family! I love designing models like this, and yall's support keeps me going. It takes a lot of time and trial runs to design new models. This model was no exception! Instructions: This model can be a bit complicated, as there are many pieces, but personally I found it very fun to assemble, and very satisfying. Step One: Connect the piston heads to the connecting rods with the two pins. Next assemble the crankshaft. This can be a bit tricky, with all the pieces looking identical, but pay attention to the photo, and you'll do fine. Note, the the position of the two cranks should be opposite, but I accidently had them the same in the first photo. The parts include are the five crankshaft pieces, three 608 bearings, the two piston assemblies, the flywheel, and one of the two gears with a hexagon cutout. Step Two: Connect the two valves to the connecting rods with the two pins. Now assemble the camshaft, this can also be a bit tricky, since there are so many pieces that make up the camshaft. Again, just pay careful attention to the photos and you'll do great. Note: If you get the crankshaft and camshaft pieces mixed up just remember the camshaft has a shorter stroke than the crankshaft, meaning the pieces are smaller. The pieces used here are the five camshaft pieces, three 608 bearings, the two valve assemblies, and one of the two gears with a hexagonal cut out. Step Three: Attach the cylinder heads to the block. There are a different amount of each size of screw included in the file, and throughout the rest of these instructions I will refer to each screw by the amount of them that are included. The set of three screws go in the three holes in a line in the head, and the single screw goes in the single hole on the other side of the head. VERY IMPORTANT: The screws included with this file are FRAGILE and cannot take very much twisting force at all. To avoid breaking off screws inside of the engine block or oil pan, finger tighten or lightly tighten with a flat-head screwdriver until its not easy and then STOP SCREWING. Note that the screwheads are also 10mm, and you may be able to fit a socket on them, but you must still be very careful to not over tighten the screws. Step Four: Now it is time to lay the crankshaft, the camshaft, and the middle gear into the engine block. This step can be tricky, and must be done correctly or the engine will not function. The secret to vacuum engines is to have the camshaft a one quarter (0.25, 90 degrees) turn AHEAD of the crankshaft, in the direction you want it to rotate. In a simpler sense, this means that while the valve is completely open (Top Dead Center) the piston must be halfway up. When the piston reaches Top Dead Center, the valve with already be half closed. Additionally, since this engine has two cylinders, the pistons and valves must be in opposite positions to be most efficient. Finally, if you would like to mess around with tuning the engine for higher speeds, try changing the amount that the camshaft leads the crankshaft. Basically, try a lead of maybe a sixth of a turn or a third of a turn, instead of a quarter turn. Step Five: Once you've got those in place, you can carefully screw the oil pan to the engine block with the set of four screws included in the file. Be sure the quarter turn amount does not change while you set the engine block and the oil pan together. Step Six: Finally, attach the exhaust manifold to the heads with the set of two screws, and the nuts. This may take some finagling to get them on. Once again remember to not overtighten, I advise only finger tightening. Congrats! Your finished! Don't forget to share a comment with a photo about your experience, I love to hear about it, whether success or failure. Also don't forget to boost!

description: Modular Articulated DNA Educational Model Let your students build, connect, and explore the DNA with this colourful modular model designed for hands-on learning. Each nucleotide piece represents one of the DNA/RNA bases, while the blue connector parts form the sugar-phosphate backbone. This model is great for classrooms, STEM projects, biology demonstrations, or anyone who wants a fun physical way to understand nucleotide pairing and DNA structure. I also plan on extending this model with a couple of more pieces for better demonstration of topics like Transcription and Translation . Feel free to leave a like and follow if you'd like to stay updated. Parts You can print as many of the individual parts as you like and connect them with each other! Each nucleotide piece represents one of the DNA/RNA bases and the blue connector parts form the sugar-phosphate backbone: Cytosine Guanine Adenine Thymine Uracil Assembly & Colouring The backbone pieces can be clicked together with a little bit of force. It is recommended to use 5x2 (dxh) magnets for both the backbone pieces and nucleotides, to better hold them in place. Place the magnets into the slot (make sure you have them oriented all in the same way!) and use a paper clip, a scredriver, or something similar to push the magnet all the way into the slot. You can also remove the magnets if needed using a paper clip from the other side. Feel free to adjust the colouring of the pieces to your needs. My file uses the colours according to the Wikipedia nucleic acid image: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleic_acid#/media/File:Difference_DNA_RNA-EN.svg Versions There are two Versions of nucleotides: Standard Set (recommended!) nucleotides have no chamfer/fillet on the connection pin. This makes them harder to separate from their counterparts, but results in a more stable double strand. Rounded Nucleotide Set contains nucleotide pieces with a rounded down connection pin. This makes them easier to separate, e.g. when demonstrating something, but obviously also reduces the stability of the entire double strand in terms of base pairs disconnecting when you move the double strand around. If you have any suggestions, feel free to let me know!

(No Bearing option Included) ⚠️ CAUTION — Please Read Before Printing or Assembling This model contains sharp edges and fine geometric features that can cause cuts or injury if handled carelessly — particularly on the fan blades and nozzle components. Please handle all parts with care during and after printing. Improper assembly may require reprinting of certain small parts. Take your time during gluing steps — rushing is the most common cause of mistakes on this build. Sections Story & Background Engine Info Printing Tips & My Modifications Assembly Instructions Final Notes 1) Story & Background This model was originally designed for a special MTU event in the DFW area — a tribute to the engineers and technicians who work on and around one of the most advanced jet engines flying today. It was built for a friend who works there, and for the incredible team around them. Building this model meant diving deep into the real engineering behind the LEAP-1B, and coming out the other side with an even deeper respect for what CFM International has achieved. It was a labor of love from first sketch to final print, and sharing it with the maker community feels like the right next step. 2) Engine Info The CFM International LEAP-1B is the exclusive powerplant for the Boeing 737 MAX , designed and produced by CFM International — a 50/50 joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines , established in 1974. It represents a massive leap forward in efficiency and sustainability over its predecessor, the CFM56. MTU & the LEAP-1B This model was created for an MTU event — and MTU's connection to this engine runs deep. MTU Aero Engines is directly involved in MRO (Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul) services for both the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B, helping keep this massive global fleet airworthy and operational. 3) Printing Tips & Modifications I made targeted modifications on a per-component basis rather than applying global settings — for example, on the engine body I adjusted print speeds for better surface quality and used support enforcers and blockers on specific areas to avoid unnecessary supports elsewhere. If you use your own print profile, you will still get a good result. However, if you have a Bambu A1 like mine, you'll get the best results using my specific print profile. Since the A1 is a Cartesian (bed-slinger) printer , outer surface quality can sometimes suffer — my speed adjustments help mitigate this, though it may not be perfect. Alternate Parts & Customization I have also uploaded an alternate parts profile for those who want additional options or a cleaner look. This includes: Clean engine variant — a version free of decals for a sleek, minimal finish Alternate display stands — additional stand styles as shown in the figures below Blank logo plates — fully blank plates that you can customize by importing SVGs directly in Bambu Studio or your preferred CAD software Bearing Options The shaft supports are designed to accommodate several bearing configurations. Choose whichever works best for you: Option Specs Notes Bambu-sourced bearing (6000ZZ) ID/OD/W: 10 × 26 × 8 mm Recommended Common Amazon bearing ID/OD/W: 8 × 22 × 7 mm Easy to source 3D printed bearing — Works, but not ideal Custom / your own bearing — Blank shaft support included Bearingless option Surprisingly works well A blank shaft support is included if you'd like to fit your own bearing or design a custom solution. All alternate parts and bearing profiles are included in the alternate parts profile attached to this upload. If you use a bearing, the shafts are pressure fit where the blade shaft diameter is 12 mm. Nozzle recommendation: I have uploaded multiple print profiles ( 0.2mm and 0.4mm). A 0.2mm nozzle will give you the best results for the lettering and logo details. 4) Assembly Instructions Step 1 — Fan Core Sub-Assembly (Shaft + Flywheel + Fan Support) Start by assembling the three core components: the blade support shaft , the flywheel , and the fan holder . Orient the shaft correctly — the flat side faces a specific direction as shown in the photo. ⚠️ If installed backwards, the fan blades will not seat in the correct position. Apply a small amount of glue into the alignment hole only — do not over-apply. Applying glue here (rather than on the shaft body) prevents glue from migrating to the shaft collar, which must remain free to spin. The completed fan core must be able to rotate freely — confirm this before the glue sets. Step 2 — Install Fan Core into Engine Body Apply glue to the designated glue area on the engine body interior as shown in the photo. Insert the fan core sub-assembly into the body. Align the notches on the shaft holder with the corresponding notches inside the engine body — this is critical for correct positioning. Do not proceed until the notches are fully seated and glue has cured. Step 3 — Fan Blades & Dowels Once the engine body assembly is fully cured, apply glue to the alignment hole of the fan blades and install them. Insert the dowels into their holes around the face ring — these may require a small amount of glue depending on fit tolerance from your printer. Step 4 — Remaining Assembly The rest of the assembly is largely self-explanatory — components are designed to fit together intuitively. Take your time and dry-fit each part before committing to glue. Step 5 — Seam Alignment (Aesthetics) For the best finished look, align the seam lines of the outer cowling sections with one another at the bottom of the engine. This small detail makes a big visual difference in the final display piece — as shown in the photo. 5) Final Notes Several customization options are included to personalize your build: Display stands — multiple styles to show off the engine Logo variants — alternate branding plates and logo options This model is shared for personal, non-commercial use only . If you are interested in selling prints of this model commercially, please leave a comment or reach out — I may look into setting up a Patreon where commercial licensing and exclusive content could be made available. As I am not personally involved in gear design and lack professional expertise in this area, the construction of this gearbox is not fully compliant with standards or industry practices in all aspects. This model requires a lot of supports! The mechanical engineering aesthetic of the parts and a support-free construction are mutually exclusive. Given that the tolerances are very tight, I recommend printing only with supports using Bambu PLA Support Material or PETG. When printing with PLA supports, quite a bit of sanding may be necessary. What this model illustrates: Adjusted mounting of Tapered Roller Bearings (in X and O arrangement) Adjustment of bearing clearance using shims and a shaft nut Assembly sequence and process utilizing housing covers What this model does not depict: Realistic, industry-standard design parameters (shaft diameters, module, screw sizes) Fit precision of components (clearance, transition, and interference fits) Realistic cast housing geometries Assembly Preparation of the Model: Embedding all Heat-Set threaded inserts into both covers and the housing. Gluing the magnets into the three machine keys and the shafts (Caution: ensure correct polarity!). Assembly Sequence: Mount the inner ring of the tapered roller bearing onto the pinion shaft. Insert the corresponding bearing outer ring into the housing bore. Insert the pinion shaft through the housing opening. Slide the inner ring of the second tapered roller bearing onto the pinion shaft. Screw the shaft nut down to secure and adjust the bearing clearance. Pre-assemble the 30mm shaft: Slide on the bevel gear and both bearing inner rings. Loosely position the pre-assembled shaft into the housing. Fasten the large housing cover. Insert the bearing outer ring on the gear side. Mount the bearing cover on the gear side (without a shim). CAUTION: This cover has a longer projection of 3 mm. Insert the second bearing outer ring on the opposite side. Insert the shim. Bearing arrangement is typically adjusted via shims of varying thickness (only realized with one shim in this model). Fasten the corresponding bearing cover. Mount the front pinion shaft cover and the end cap for the pinion shaft on the opposite side. Insert all shaft seals (optionally, these can also be glued in before mounting the covers). Insert the machine keys.

This is a 3d printable self centering lathe chuck. It is a great tool for your everyday machinist, or simply as a decoration for those fond of lathes and how they work. This model is great to help you understand how a self centering lathe chuck works. It can also be used for educational purposes where it can help others better grasp the concept of printed mechanical assemblies. This is a model that most definitely needs support, and also a high infill and number of walls in some of the parts. Especially the bolts and the key. The key itself functions both as to make the chuck work, by being the driving force behind the whole mechanism. And it also a hex key allowing you to tighten the bolts, though not too hard, since they are printed, and cant wihstand that much pressure without snapping. VERY IMPORTANT !!! When assembling the lathe chuck you have to ake sure you do it in the right order, or else the chuck will not grip around the center. You have to put claw 1 in slot 1 and so forth. When the claws sit in their respective slots, you need to turn the key, until they all get gripped by the spiral. You NEED to make sure that claw one grips first, then claw two, and lastly claw 3. This will make sure that the self centering mechanism works. When the claws have gotten grip, you simply turn it until the claws slowly move inwards. You will very likely need a bit of force to get the claws moving inwards. I recommend sliding the claws back and forth in their respective slots, when the spiral isnt in. This will help break in the slots, and make sure they move more smoothly. Video Of Assembly I hope you like the model, and have a fun time printing and using it. -Sincerely Capspam3D.

description: This is a functional, 100% human-engineered mechanical demonstration piece showcasing a massive 2,023,680:1 total reduction ratio through a custom nested strain wave drive system. It is designed to be fully 3D printed with minimal hardware required, making it a highly accessible build that visually breaks down complex mechanical engineering. It includes a custom base to display the final assembly while it runs. The Math (Gear Ratios) The extreme reduction is achieved through four nested stages: Stage 1 : 40:42 (20:1) Stage 2 : 68:70 (34:1) Stage 3 : 96:98 (48:1) Stage 4 : 124:126 (62:1) Bill of Materials (BOM) All printed components (including display stand) 1x USB TT Motor 2x 2.5x6mm machine screws (Note: These are the exact same screws used in the Cyber Brick build) Lubricant (for the flexsplines) Assembly Instructions Mount the Motor: Install the USB TT motor into the assembly and secure it with the motor housing using the two 2.5x6mm machine screws. Install Wave Guides: Snap the wave guides (top gear portions) securely into their designated places. Prep the Flexsplines: Apply lubricant to the smooth side of the flexsplines (the flexible rings). Seat the Flexsplines: Carefully install the lubricated flexsplines into their appropriately sized channels. Final Drive: Press the wave generator onto the TT Motor shaft.

NEMA 17 High-Torque 2-Stage Planetary Gearbox (1:25 Ratio) This is a compact and robust 2-stage planetary gearbox specifically designed for NEMA 17 stepper motors . With a total reduction ratio of 1:25 , it provides a significant torque boost for your robotics projects, actuators, or DIY automation. The design is optimized for 3D printing, featuring easy-to-identify parts and a straightforward assembly process. Technical Specifications: Total Gear Ratio: 1:25 Motor Compatibility: NEMA 17 Stepper Motor Bearings: 8x (10x5x4mm) Fasteners: M3x30mm screws & M3 Heat-set inserts Reduction Mechanism: Dual-stage planetary gears Bill of Materials (BOM): To complete this build, you will need: Bearings: 8 pieces of 10x5x4mm (standard MR105 or similar). Screws: 4x M3x30mm bolts. Inserts: 4x M3 heat-set inserts (to be installed in the motor mount housing). Key Design Features: Error-Proof Assembly: To prevent confusion during assembly, the Stage 1 Ring Gear is narrower than the Stage 2 Ring Gear. Always use the thinner ring for the first stage (closer to the motor). Secure Mounting: All stages are held together by M3x30mm screws that thread directly into heat-set inserts melted into the motor mount for maximum durability. Assembly Instructions: Preparation: Press the M3 heat-set inserts into the dedicated holes on the Motor Mount . Stage 1: Press-fit the Stage 1 Sun Gear onto the NEMA 17 motor shaft. Install the Narrower Ring Gear onto the motor mount. Place the Stage 1 Planet Carrier (with bearings and planet gears installed). Stage 2: The Stage 2 Sun Gear should be mounted onto the Output Shaft (which connects the two stages). Install the Wider Ring Gear for Stage 2. Place the Stage 2 Planet Carrier. Final Step: Place the Top Cover Plate and secure the entire assembly using the four M3x30mm screws . Tighten them evenly into the inserts in the motor mount. description: This is a 2 part wall mount for an Artemis SLS model rocket. It is designed for a 1:100 scale which would be a model approximately 98 cm or 38.6" tall. The lower base has 2 pegs which are designed to stabilize the solid rocket booster engines from slipping off the base. The pegs are 5-3/16" (13.18cm) center to center and ½" (12.7mm) in diameter. This design is meant to accommodate various versions of the model and not be a tight fit but simply be a guard rail of sorts to prevent the model from being shaken or bumped off the mount. The upper bracket has 2 arms which can be printed in the color of the central orange core stage. The arms articulate in rather stiff pivots to hold the model firmly. They will adapt to variations in scale, but for reference, they are approximately 3 inches (76mm) in diameter when fully closed. To assemble the arms on the upper mount, simply push the arm onto the peg to get it started, then flip it over and put the joint over the edge of a table or kitchen counter and press down firmly to push the mount into the arm. If you have difficulty getting one or both arms started, you may need to file or sand the inside corner of the arm hole to remove a burr that may have printed. I found this was required on one arm I tested. The arm will sit flush when installed and be tight, yet it will move. To prevent breakage of the arm, open and close the mount by applying force close to the pivot point, not from the outer ends of the arm as it may snap. The joint should be stiff. Opening and closing it repeatedly will loosen the fit. The model may be removed from its mount by simply opening the arms in this manner. Your print or download are greatly appreciated. You can follow this video below for specs, know how it works and assemble the grenade. Airsoft Impact Spring Grenade The performance of the grenade is heavily linked to the springs, I wouldn't go higher than 50mm for the AEG spring (I used a stock one) because I see no real benefit for it. As for the trapezoidal (mid cap) springs, the best quality you can find, the better. I used the springs from a Cyma mid cap 140bb mag but I believe Maple Leaf sells a "better" spring kit for mid-caps for around 15€ so if you are going to invest, you may want to consider in that possibility. If you end up using the Maple Leaf ones or any possible better springs, please do let me know. As for the 4mm pen springs, as long as it's around 4mm in diameter and compresses enough for the traps to compress and let the BBs through, it should be good. Hardware needed: - 1 AEG Spring (or similar) cut to 40-50mm (length will depend on your spring strengh) - 1 Mid-cap (140bbs) or 1 trapezoidal spring cut to 6 sections of 90mm - 2 4mm pen springs cut to 6 sections of 4-5mm (don't use the ends, it might not compress enough= - 13 M2x8 bolts (M2x6 can also work but I'd rather use the x8) - 1 1.5mm allen key to be used as a pin or anything you want to use instead I've given 0.3mm tolerance overall between parts but sanding might be needed for optimal performance. You want the BB to go through smoothly and every part to slide well. All that while not having a huge play between parts either. The skin (printed in TPU) is optional but highly recommended for durability, knowing this is something you'll be throwing around. If something is to break in the interior, it's more likely to be the piston shaft due to the middle section thickness, so this is one of the reasons why I wouldn't over do the spring length, more length means more power but it also means more stress, and in this case, more power wouldn't give you better results. The skin also serves an aesthetic purpose, so I'd like to have more variety in the future. If you have a design in mind and can't model it, send me some sketches with the precise idea (possibly with precise dimensions too) and I'll be happy for model and join it to the STLs. Leave your feedback and questions in the comments.

🧊 The ultimate customizable 3D shape generator! Need physical geometry manipulatives for a math class? Looking to create custom building blocks for your kids, or test out your printer's dimensional accuracy? This fully parametric OpenSCAD generator instantly creates 13 different mathematically perfect 3D solid shapes at any dimension you require. Membership Educational manipulatives and custom building blocks are great tools for schools and parents. While this basic geometric generator is freely available, joining my Commercial Membership for only €4.99/mo gives you full commercial rights to sell physical prints of this model, AND unlocks commercial rights to ALL my other premium generators! ⚙️ Customizer features: 13 classic volumes: Instantly render a cube, cuboid, cylinder, sphere, cone, truncated cone, torus, triangular prism, hexagonal prism, square pyramid, triangular pyramid, capsule, or ellipsoid. Mass batch generation: Select All Shapes Grid from the dropdown to instantly generate a perfectly spaced classroom layout of all 13 shapes on your build plate at once! Make it hollow: Enable Make_Hollow and specify a wall thickness. This automatically hollows out the top of the shape, turning it into an open cup or container. This is perfect for teaching volume in math class by filling them with water or sand! Infinite sizing: Enter your exact X, Y, and Z dimensions to stretch and scale the shapes dynamically. 🧠 Behind the design (For makers & moderators) To provide the absolute fastest rendering performance, this model uses dynamic parameter mapping. Instead of importing separate complex meshes, the algorithm manipulates the core OpenSCAD primitive functions. For example, prisms and pyramids are mathematically generated by taking a standard cylinder and dynamically overriding its face resolution ($fn) to 3, 4, or 6, instantly turning it into a sharp geometric solid. The Make_Hollow function utilizes a smart boolean difference, dynamically duplicating the chosen shape, shrinking it precisely by the user-defined wall thickness, and subtracting it from the original solid exactly at the top plane. 🖨️ Print settings: Material: PLA is perfect for educational blocks. Layer height: 0.20mm works beautifully. If you are printing the sphere or ellipsoid, 0.16mm will make the top curves much smoother. Supports: Mostly none. description: Overview This soccer kinetic sculpture has linkages that cause the ball to always be centered in the exact same position. It is a themed version of the model you can find here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2961089-fixed-center-kinetic-sculpture-floating-ball#profileId-3319236 All of the parts in this model are compatible with the parts in the original. Due to each hinge axis passing through the center, no matter how each link is moved, it will cause the entire structure to articulate around a stationary center. It features a print-in-place and thread-together design that requires no glue or additional hardware. It requires no supports and is extremely fascinating and satisfying. The base can also be filled with sand or other materials to provide a more premium feel. For printing Standard setting can be used for printing. No AMS is required and no supports are needed. Two versions of the ball are available. One that requires an AMS or dual nozzle and one that requires the pentagons to be pressed or glued into place. For the print profiles, there is one with all parts on separate plates with both types of balls in the profile and two that have all the parts on a single plate (one includes the funnel and the other does not). All materials should work; however, for the ball to stay more centered, avoid flexible materials like TPU. Features The model prints in three or fourteen pieces: the base, the print-in-place linkages, and the ball that requires AMS or the ball that does not and the eleven pentagons. Additionally, a funnel can be printed to more easily fill the base with sand or another material. The hole for filling the base is the same hole that the linkage structure threads into. The entire structure is about 95 mm in diameter and about 105 mm tall. All of these parts are completely compatible with the original model. https://makerworld.com/en/models/2961089-fixed-center-kinetic-sculpture-floating-ball#profileId-3319236 Assembly Assembling this model is very simple. Optionally, the funnel can be threaded into the hole in the base and the base filled. After the funnel is removed, the linkage structure can be threaded into that same hole until it stops. The location of where the threads stop should position the linkage structure properly. If the no-AMS ball is printed, the pentagons need to be placed in place (they will likely require some glue). Lastly, the ball can be threaded onto the rod at the center of the ring. The links may be slightly stiff and not want to move after printing, but with some slight pressure, the links can be broken free. Other Versions with Themes This is a variation that I created of my original model. https://makerworld.com/en/models/2961089-fixed-center-kinetic-sculpture-floating-ball#profileId-3319236 I currently plan on making more variations of this model with other specific themes. These may include but not be limited to: A space theme with the ball being a planet or the moon. A version themed around a different sport such as basketball, baseball, tennis, golf, volleyball, or American football. A moving object-themed version that could be a motorcycle, racecar, airplane, or rocket. An outdoor activity-themed version that could have a surfboard, skateboard, or fishing bobber or lure. A larger version that had a light using the led light kit. There are many possible versions that I could create. Let me know which ones you want to see, and let me know of any other ideas that you have. Other notes If you have any questions or comments, feel free to ask in the comments or send me a private message.

My Educational Mechanical Examples Series This model is one of my educational mechanical mechanism examples on 80mm x 80mm base plates. You can find all models of the series in this collection => [Mechanical Mechanism Examples] The present model This is an educational model of a Hart's A-frame, which is one of the exact straight-line linkages. Brief Description The approximate straight-line mechanisms introduced so far — Watt's linkage, the Chebyshev linkage, and the Grasshopper linkage — are all based on four-bar linkages. The coupler point need not lie at a joint between two links; it may sit at the midpoint of a link or on its extension. Even so, these simple linkages confine the coupler point to a path that is only approximately straight — and they do so without any linear guide or prismatic pair. A four-bar linkage, however, cannot trace an exactly straight line. Hart's A-frame achieves exact straight-line motion by raising the number of links to six. Five of them move; the sixth is the base plate itself, which serves as the hidden ground link. Laid out as the capital letter A, each slanted side is built from a long link and a short link half its length, joined end to end, and the two short links meet at the apex. The lower end of each long link is pinned to the base plate, and these two fixed pivots are spaced apart by twice the length of the crossbar. The crossbar — the horizontal stroke of the A — joins the two long links at the points that divide them in a 3:1 ratio, with the longer portion toward the fixed pivot. Only these two lower pivots are anchored; every other joint is free to move. Under this arrangement the apex of the A, which is the coupler point, is constrained to travel along a perfectly straight line: the vertical line engraved on the base plate, which is the perpendicular bisector of the two fixed pivots. Move the coupler point by hand and you can feel it being held to this line. As you play with the model, though, you will find that this is not the only path open to the coupler point: the motion branches at the midpoint between the two pivots. There, the coupler point can leave the straight line for a second, skewed path that traces a distorted triangle, also engraved on the plate. Pushing on the coupler point alone will not carry it past the corners of that triangle; there you must also control how the links fold in order to pass through. To keep the motion well-behaved, confine the coupler point to either the upper or the lower half of the straight line, or guide it through the midpoint so that it does not slip onto the other branch. Reference https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart%27s_inversors Related Models Case This model is compatible with the case included in my first set . Printing Use the models named ???-printable.stl for printing . The models named ???-assembled.stl are provided just to show how they should be assembled. Use well-dried PETG to have better dimensional accuracy. Use 0.1 mm or 0.08 mm layer height to have smoother surfaces. Use slow printing speed for overhangs. Select “Random” seam position to have smoother rotation. Randomly distributed seam should be easily worn out after some wearing.Printing Sanding and Filing Note that, in this model, the rotation of the bases for bearings is intentionally made not too smooth. Sometimes, the gears suffer from the stringing effect and/or elephant foot effect, resulting in a too tight fit to the shafts (they are designed with a 0.15 mm radial clearance). If you see rough surface on the shafts due to stringing, sand off the roughness with a small piece of sand paper. If you feel the gears do not rotate smoothly due to an elephant effect, widen the hole slightly by using a thin round bar file. Without those issues, the parts should rotate very smoothly with minimal friction. Assembly Secure the links onto the shafts with the retaining rings. LouVee Air Car V2 - Rubber Band Powered Wind Spinner Car A fully 3D-printed LouVee air car redesigned for the Wind Spinner Design Contest as a more functional, reliable, and classroom-friendly build. The model only needs rubber bands to run and demonstrates stored energy, airflow, friction, motion, and basic mechanical design in a simple hands-on way. This V2 keeps the recognizable LouVee air car concept, but the design has been rebuilt for better performance and easier printing. The biggest change is the new press-and-lock wheel and shaft system, which makes assembly easier, keeps the wheels better aligned, and fixes the drift issue from the earlier version. As a result, the car travels much straighter when propelled. The updated parts use less filament, print faster, and are less prone to breaking, especially around the wheel shafts. The cleaner geometry also makes the model more repeatable for classroom use, STEM demonstrations, or anyone wanting a simple rubber-band-powered engineering project. The propeller is powered by twisted rubber bands. The notches allow for different rubber band sizes and tension levels. After testing one rubber band and two bands side by side, I found that tying two rubber bands together stores more usable energy and gives the car better performance overall. To use the car, twist the propeller counter-clockwise. When released, it spins clockwise, pushes air backward, and moves the car forward. The body is kept lightweight so the airflow can propel it effectively while still being strong enough for repeated use. Main Improvements in V2 Redesigned as a functional contest entry New press-and-lock wheel and shaft mechanism Much easier wheel assembly Fixed wheel drift for straighter motion Lighter design with less filament use Faster print time Stronger and less break-prone wheel shafts Assembly: The Assembly is simple. First take your wheel shafts and insert them into the main body in their respective short and long holes. Then press the wheel into the holes with the larger ones going in the back. You may need to push the wheels a bit outward to straighten them out once in the body. Then take the Shaft with a hook and put it through the D shaped hole in the proppeler with the hood in the side with more distance toward the blades. Then insert it into the Cylinder of the main body. Finally, tie two rubber bands together, and put one in the hook of the propeller, and the other in the hook of the main body that better tensions the car. Spin counterclockwise and enjoy! (note it may take a good amount of spins before the wind is strong enough to propell the car forward)

Number Nine’s Whistle 1/3 scale 3d printed model This is a model of the single chime locomotive whistle on WW&F #9 that you enjoy hearing echoing through the woods of Alna, Maine. The actual whistle is a replica made by volunteers at the railway. It was created based on drawings by the Portland Company (Portland, Maine) who built the locomotive in 1891 for the Sandy River Railway. I used the original drawings to create this little whistle model. It is printed in PLA plastic on my Bambu A1. It is somewhat delicate and may not be ideal for small children, it also takes quite a bit of breath to toot! It is higher pitched than the full-size steam whistle on the locomotive but that is physics. Wiscasset Waterville and Farmington Railway Museum wwfry.org 97 Cross Road, Alna, Maine 04535 Printing is 5 parts. the bell is the largest. I have a Bambu A1. I print them as offered in the file with good success, feel free to try other orientations. I use 4 wall loops for strength. I print at 33% you can try other scales; bigger takes more breath and is lower pitched, smaller is easier to blow and higher pitched. The post has been adjusted so that it fits the other parts as printed at 33%. ASSEMBLY: -Clean out the support material. the base is a little fussy to get the material out of; I use a sharp poky thing, like a nail. Try not to damage the thin outer edge. -Insert the round plate, flat side out, into the base. -Insert the post into the base so that the flange holds the plate down. -Slide the bell down onto the other end of the post until it stops. you should have about a 5mm or ¼" space at the bottom. -slide the nut on to the post on top of the bell. -give it a toot!

model_name: Plaster Molds for Kids Painting – Dino Edition
description: 🚨 Selling my prints? If you want to sell physical 3D prints of my designs, please hit the "Follow" button! I will be launching the Commercial License Membership very soon! 🚀 2.5 D Plaster Molds Dino🦖🎨 Turn your 3D printer into a never-ending factory for creative toys! Are you looking for a great weekend activity to keep your kids entertained for hours? This project perfectly combines 3D printing technology with classic hands-on crafting. Anyone who has tried letting kids paint a standard 3D printed model (made of PLA or PETG) with watercolours or tempera knows it’s a struggle – the paint slides off the plastic surface, runs, and doesn't cover well. Plaster casts made from these TPU molds are a complete game-changer. Plaster has the perfect absorbency, so colors stick flawlessly, dry instantly, and look incredibly vibrant. You only need to print these flexible molds once, and you can cast plaster dinosaurs for your kids every single weekend, over and over again. 💡 Why TPU 95A? These molds are designed specifically for printing with TPU 95A flexible filament. Thanks to the unique compliance of this material, you don't have to worry about complex mold-release draft angles during modeling. The model is designed with an optimal wall thickness of 1.5 mm , which provides the perfect balance: the mold keeps its geometry perfectly and doesn't bulge under the weight of liquid plaster, yet it remains flexible enough that you can incredibly easily peel it off the hardened cast like a banana skin. No getting stuck, no broken details. 🛠️ Recommended Print Settings: Material: TPU 95A (e.g., Bambu TPU). Wall Thickness / Perimeters: 3 walls (crucial for maintaining the mold's stability). Infill: 10%. Note: Print directly from the rear spool holder of your printer, do NOT use the AMS , as flexible materials tend to get tangled and stuck in it! For a perfectly smooth inner surface, make sure your TPU is well dried before printing. 🧪 Step-by-Step Casting Guide for Kids: Preparation: Place the clean and dry TPU mold on a flat, stable surface. Pro Trick for Zero Bubbles: Lightly spray the inside of the mold with a spray bottle filled with water and a single drop of regular dish soap. The soap acts as a wetting agent – it lowers surface tension, allowing the plaster to flow flawlessly into the smallest details without leaving air bubbles on the surface. Alternatively, you can use a release agent made of wax dissolved in alcohol. Mixing the Plaster: Mix standard white hobby plaster with water according to the package instructions. Make sure to mix the consistency a bit thinner (like runny pancake batter) – this is very important to ensure the plaster flows easily and without resistance into all the fine details and crevices of the dinosaur. Pouring: Carefully pour the plaster into the mold. It is recommended to leave about 2–3 mm from the top rim for easier handling. Once poured, gently tap the mold against the table a couple of times (vibration) to release any remaining trapped air bubbles to the surface. Releasing the Mold: Wait about 20 to 30 minutes. Once the plaster is solid and warm to the touch (due to the exothermic reaction), gently peel the TPU mold away by bending it. Thanks to the 1.5 mm thin wall, it will come off effortlessly. Creative Finale: Let the cast dry completely (ideally in the sun or on a radiator until it turns bright white and "rings" when tapped). Then, just give your kids brushes, tempera, or acrylic paints and let them create!
